abstract: Conversations among friends are often more dynamic, enjoyable, and wide-ranging than those between strangers. How do friends do this? We propose that inside jokes, shared experiences, and mutual interests give friends an aligned mental map, allowing them to leap between topics without losing each other. Strangers may begin in separate mental landscapes, limiting opportunities for exploration as they take smaller steps to avoid confusion. To test these possibilities, we tracked the dyadic dynamics of friends (n = 60) and strangers (n = 54) as they engaged in a real-time conversation using fMRI hyperscanning. We employed Hyper-Hidden-Markov-Modeling to project partner's neural states into a shared latent space and to segment them into discrete events. This allowed us to quantify how similarly each dyad represented each event (representational alignment), and how spread out conversational events were in latent space (representational exploration). We tested how neural alignment predicted exploration, how both neural measures relate to the breadth of topics discussed, and how they predicted the subjective experience of the conversation quality in friends and strangers. We found that the more a dyad aligned neurally, the more they also explored. While both neural alignment and exploration predicted the breadth of conversations, only neural exploration predicted better perceived conversation quality. Friends were more neurally aligned, which was associated with more exploration. Thus, when friends brains represent the world more similarly to each other, they tend to embark on more diverse and far-reaching conversations spanning a broader range of topics, all while staying anchored in common ground.
